questions.question: Isotopes are atoms of an element that have different: A electronic structures, B numbers of electrons, C numbers of protons, D numbers of neutrons.
steps: Isotopes have the same number of protons, so the same atomic number and element.
Neutral isotopes therefore have the same number of electrons and the same electronic structure.
They differ only in mass number, which means a different number of neutrons.

questions.question: Which is the electronic configuration of the Sc3+ ion? A 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6; B 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5 3d1; C 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d1 4s2; D 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d4 4s2.
steps: Sc has 21 electrons: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d1 4s2.
Positive ions lose electrons from the 4s subshell first, then from 3d.
Sc3+ loses 4s2 and 3d1 (3 electrons), leaving 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6.

questions.question: Which element is in the d-block of the Periodic Table? A argon, B chlorine, C iron, D sodium.
steps: A d-block element has its last electron in a d subshell.
Argon and chlorine are p-block, sodium is s-block.
Iron (Fe, [Ar] 3d6 4s2) is in the d-block.

questions.question: Which is the equation for the second ionisation energy of element A? A A(g) -> A2+(g) + 2e-; B A+(g) -> A2+(g) + e-; C A2+(g) -> A3+(g) + e-; D A2+(g) -> A4+(g) + 2e-.
steps: The second ionisation removes one electron from the 1+ ion.
Reactant must be A+(g), product A2+(g) plus one electron.
Option B matches.

questions.question: The mass spectrum of a sample of silicon is shown. What is the best estimate for the relative atomic mass? Options A 28.0, B 28.2, C 28.8, D 29.0.
steps: Read the relative abundances from the peak heights: 28Si is by far the largest (about 90%), 29Si about 6% and 30Si about 4%.
Relative atomic mass = sum of (m/z x abundance) / sum of abundances, which is a weighted mean.
Option A (28.0) ignores the heavier isotopes; B (28.2) is the closest estimate.

questions.question: Using the diagram of first ionisation energies from sodium to silicon, what is the approximate first ionisation energy (kJ mol-1) of phosphorus (atomic number 15)? Options A 400, B 500, C 700, D 1000.
steps: The graph gives Na 500, Mg about 740, Al about 580 and Si about 790 kJ mol^-1.
Across Period 3 the first ionisation energy generally rises because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays the same.
Phosphorus follows silicon, so its value must be above 790; 400, 500 and 700 are all too low, leaving 1000 kJ mol^-1.

questions.question: Which is the electronic configuration of a carbon atom in its ground state? (Options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Carbon has 6 electrons (atomic number 6).
Fill the lowest energy orbitals first: 1s2, then 2s2.
The last 2 electrons go into 2p, singly in separate orbitals (Hund's rule).

questions.question: The first six ionisation energies (kJ mol-1) of an element are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 578, 14 831 and 18 378. Which group includes this element? Options A Group 2, B Group 3, C Group 4, D Group 5.
steps: Large jump between the 3rd (2745) and 4th (11 578) ionisation energies.
The jump shows that the first three electrons are outer electrons and the 4th comes from a full inner shell.
Three outer electrons means Group 3 (as labelled in the options).

questions.question: What is the maximum number of electrons in the 3p subshell, and in the third quantum shell of an atom?
questions.answer: 6 electrons in 3p; 18 electrons in the third shell
steps: The p subshell has 3 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so 3p holds 6.
The third shell (n = 3) holds 2n2 = 18 electrons (3s 2 + 3p 6 + 3d 10).
Each orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons with opposite spins.

questions.question: The hydroxide ion, OH-, has a total of 9 protons. How many neutrons and electrons are there in this ion? (Mass numbers are not given; use the common isotopes 16O and 1H.)
steps: OH- has 8 protons from O and 1 from H, total 9 protons, as given.
OH- carries a 1- charge, so electrons = protons + 1 = 10.
Common isotopes: 16O has 8 neutrons and 1H has none, so there are 8 neutrons.

questions.question: A sample of silicon contains the isotopes shown (not included in the extracted text). What is the relative atomic mass to one decimal place? Options A 28.0, B 28.2, C 29.0, D 29.8.
steps: To one decimal place this is 28.2.

questions.question: The decrease in first ionisation energy down Group 1 is caused by the increase in: A force of attraction between the nucleus and outer electron, B number of neutrons in the nucleus, C number of protons in the nucleus, D shielding of the outer electron from the nuclear charge.
steps: Going down Group 1, the outer electron is in a higher shell.
More inner shells increase shielding from the nuclear charge.
The outer electron is held less strongly and is removed more easily, so IE falls.

questions.question: What is the equation for the third ionisation energy of aluminium? A Al(g) -> Al3+(g) + 3e-; B Al(s) -> Al3+(s) + 3e-; C Al2+(g) -> Al3+(g) + e-; D Al2+(s) -> Al3+(s) + e-.
steps: The nth ionisation energy removes one electron from the (n-1)+ ion, in the gas phase.
Third IE: Al2+(g) -> Al3+(g) + e-.
Options A and B remove all three at once or use solid state; D uses solid state.

questions.question: Using the chart of first ionisation energies from fluorine to magnesium, what is the approximate first ionisation energy (kJ mol-1) of aluminium? Options A 300, B 600, C 900, D 1200.
steps: From the chart: F about 1680, Ne about 2080, Na about 500, Mg about 740 kJ mol^-1.
Aluminium is the next element after Mg, and Al has a lower first ionisation energy than Mg because its outer electron is in a 3p subshell, which is higher in energy and shielded by the 3s electrons.
So it falls below 740 but stays above Na (500): about 580 to 600 kJ mol^-1, which is option B.

questions.question: The first three ionisation energies of carbon are shown (table not included in the extracted text). Which is the approximate fourth ionisation energy? Options A 3500, B 6200, C 11 000, D 38 000.
steps: The values given are 1086, 2353 and 4621 kJ mol^-1: each successive ionisation energy rises steadily because electrons come from the same shell and the remaining ions are more charged.
Carbon has 4 outer-shell electrons (2s2 2p2), so the 4th is also from the n = 2 shell and follows the steady pattern: about 6200.
The huge jump to about 38 000 comes at the 5th ionisation, when an electron is removed from the inner 1s shell; 3500 would be lower than the 3rd value.

questions.question: The two stable isotopes of bromine have relative masses 79 and 81. Which is the correct pattern of peaks in the mass spectrum of molecular bromine? (The peak diagrams are not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: D (small peaks at 79 and 81, and three molecular-ion peaks at 158, 160 and 162 in the ratio 1:2:1)
steps: Br2 contains two atoms, each 79Br or 81Br with roughly equal abundance.
Molecular ions: 79Br79Br (158), 79Br81Br (160, two ways to make it) and 81Br81Br (162), so peaks in the ratio 1:2:1 with the middle one tallest.
Fragmentation also gives small Br+ peaks at 79 and 81 of equal height, which are shown in all four options.
Only D shows a tall central peak at 160 with equal peaks either side.

questions.question: Which statement about subatomic particles is correct? A neutral atoms always contain the same number of protons and electrons; B neutral atoms always contain the same number of protons and neutrons; C electrons have a relative mass of 1 and a charge of -1; D protons have a relative mass of 1 and no charge.
questions.answer: A (neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons)
steps: A neutral atom has no overall charge, so electrons balance protons.
B is wrong because neutron number varies between isotopes.
C is wrong: electrons have negligible relative mass (about 1/1840), and D is wrong: protons have charge +1.

questions.question: The bar chart shows the melting temperatures of the first twenty elements. Which statement is shown? A giant covalent structures highest in Period 2 and Period 3; B metals always higher than non-metals; C increase going down each group; D increase across Period 2 and Period 3. (The chart is not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: A: giant covalent structures have the highest melting temperatures in Period 2 and Period 3
steps: In Period 2 the highest bar is element 6 (carbon, diamond or graphite) and in Period 3 it is element 14 (silicon); both are giant covalent.
B is wrong: some non-metals (carbon) melt higher than metals, and lithium and sodium (metals) are low.
C is wrong: the Group 1 values fall from Li to Na to K.
D is wrong: the melting temperatures rise then fall across each period, not steadily.

questions.question: Which sketch graph shows the trend in first ionisation energy going down Group 1? (The sketch options are not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: A: a steady fall in first ionisation energy, levelling off
steps: Going down Group 1 the outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is more shielded, so less energy is needed to remove it.
The first ionisation energy therefore decreases smoothly (520, 496, 419, 403, 376 kJ mol^-1) with smaller falls lower down, as in graph A.
B rises, C stays high then drops suddenly and D falls with an irregular kink, none of which fits a regular group trend.

questions.question: Which ion does not have the electronic configuration shown? Options A K+, B Ca2+, C Ti2+, D Sc3+. (The configuration shown in the question is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: The diagram shows 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6, a total of 18 electrons.
K+ (19 - 1), Ca2+ (20 - 2) and Sc3+ (21 - 3) each have 18 electrons.
Ti2+ has 22 - 2 = 20 electrons, so it also has 3d2 and does not match.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of the nitride ion, N3-? A 1s2 2s2; B 1s2 2s2 2p3; C 1s2 2s2 2p4; D 1s2 2s2 2p6.
steps: Nitrogen has 7 electrons; N3- gains 3, giving 10 electrons.
So N3- is 1s2 2s2 2p6, option D.

questions.question: The mass spectrum of a sample of an element is shown. What is the Ar of the element? Options A 42.0, B 48.0, C 63.6, D 64.0.
steps: The main peaks are at m/z = 63 (abundance about 46) and m/z = 65 (about 20).
The small peaks at 31.5 and 32.5 are 63Cu2+ and 65Cu2+, in the same ratio, so they do not change the average.

questions.question: Which species could be responsible for the peak at m/z = 32.5? Options A 32S+, B 63Cu2+, C 65Cu2+, D 98Tc3+.
steps: m/z = mass / charge.
Check the others: 32S+ gives 32; 63Cu2+ gives 31.5; 98Tc3+ gives 32.7.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term orbital.
questions.answer: A region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability (about 90 to 95%) of finding an electron; an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
steps: An orbital is a region of space, not a fixed path.
It is the region where an electron is likely to be found (high probability, about 90 to 95%).
Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.

questions.question: State the shape of an s orbital and the shape of a p orbital.
questions.answer: s orbital is spherical; p orbital is dumbbell-shaped (two lobes)
steps: An s orbital is symmetrical about the nucleus, so it is spherical.
A p orbital has two lobes on either side of the nucleus, a dumbbell shape.

questions.question: Describe what can be deduced about the electronic structure of sodium from its successive ionisation energies.
questions.answer: Sodium has one outer (3s) electron, then a large jump after removing it, showing 8 electrons in the second shell and 2 in the first, so 2,8,1.
steps: The first IE is low, so there is one electron in the outer shell.
The big jump occurs after the first electron is removed, since the next electron comes from a full inner shell.
Count the electrons before the jump: 1 outer electron, then 8 in the second shell and 2 in the first shell (2,8,1).

questions.question: Plot a graph of the log of the fourth ionisation energy for six elements given in the table.
questions.answer: Graph of log10(fourth ionisation energy) against element: points at O 3.87, F 3.92, Ne 3.97, Mg 4.02 and Al 4.06, with a straight line of best fit (rising by about 0.04 to 0.05 per element)
steps: Put the elements in order of atomic number along the x-axis (O 8, F 9, Ne 10, Na 11, Mg 12, Al 13), one large square per element, labelled "element" or "atomic number".
Label the y-axis "log10 (fourth ionisation energy / kJ mol^-1)" with a scale of about 3.80 to 4.10 (0.05 per large square) so the points fill the grid.
Plot the five known points accurately: (O, 3.87), (F, 3.92), (Ne, 3.97), (Mg, 4.02), (Al, 4.06); Na is left for part (ii).
Draw one straight line of best fit through the points; it passes through the Na position at about 3.99 to 4.00.

questions.question: Use your graph to estimate the fourth ionisation energy of sodium, in kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: About 1.0 x 10^4 kJ mol^-1 (log value about 3.99 to 4.00; accept roughly 9800 to 10 000)
steps: Read the log10 value for Na (between Ne at 3.97 and Mg at 4.02) from the line of best fit: about 3.995.
Fourth ionisation energy = 10^3.995 = about 9900 kJ mol^-1, i.e. about 1.0 x 10^4 kJ mol^-1.

questions.question: Suggest why the fourth ionisation energies of neon and sodium are similar in magnitude, even though they are in different periods.
questions.answer: The fourth electron removed from each comes from the second quantum shell (n = 2), with similar shielding and effective nuclear charge.
steps: For Na the 4th electron is removed from the 2p subshell (n = 2), since its 3s electron has already gone.
For Ne the 4th electron is also removed from the 2p subshell (n = 2).
Both electrons are in the same shell, with similar shielding and nuclear charge, so the energies are similar.

questions.question: Which equation represents the third ionisation energy for element J? A J2+(g) -> J3+(g) + e-; B J3+(g) -> J4+(g) + e-; C J(g) -> J3+(g) + e-; D J(g) -> J3+(g) + 3e-.
steps: Ionisation number n removes one electron from the (n-1)+ ion.
For the third IE, the ion starts as J2+ and ends as J3+.
Only option A matches.

questions.question: Complete the table to show the numbers of subatomic particles in 56Fe2+.
steps: Iron has atomic number 26, so 26 protons.
Neutrons = mass number - protons = 56 - 26 = 30.
Fe2+ has lost 2 electrons, so electrons = 26 - 2 = 24.

questions.question: A sample of iron contains the following isotopes (data not included in the extracted text). Calculate the relative atomic mass to three significant figures.
steps: The abundances sum to 100% (5.84 + 91.68 + 2.17 + 0.31).
To 3 s.f. the relative atomic mass is 55.9.

questions.question: Magnesium reacts with aqueous iron(II) sulfate in a displacement reaction. Write the ionic equation, including state symbols.
steps: Mg is more reactive than Fe, so it displaces iron from Fe2+(aq).
Mg loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+; Fe2+ gains 2 electrons to form Fe(s).
Charges balance: left 2+, right 2+; atoms balance.

questions.question: A compound of 25.00 g contains 6.98 g of iron and 6.03 g of sulfur; the rest is oxygen. Calculate its empirical formula. Ar: O 16.0, S 32.1, Fe 55.8.
steps: Divide by 0.1251: Fe 1 : S 1.50 : O 5.99, which gives 2 : 3 : 12.
Empirical formula Fe2S3O12, i.e. Fe2(SO4)3.

questions.question: 6.95 g of FeSO4.xH2O is heated and produces 2.00 g Fe2O3, 0.80 g SO2 and 1.00 g SO3, with water as the only other product. Deduce the overall equation, showing working. Ar: H 1.0, O 16.0, S 32.1, Fe 55.8.
steps: Fe in products = 2 x 0.0125 = 0.0250 mol, so FeSO4 = 0.0250 mol; S in products = 0.0125 + 0.0125 = 0.0250 mol, which matches.
Mass of FeSO4 = 0.0250 x 151.9 = 3.80 g, so the water mass = 6.95 - 3.80 = 3.15 g.
Moles H2O = 3.15 / 18.0 = 0.175 mol, which is 7 H2O per FeSO4 (x = 7).
Balance per 2 FeSO4.7H2O: 2FeSO4.7H2O -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3 + 14H2O.

questions.question: Which ion has the electronic configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 in its ground state? A Al3+, B Cl-, C N3-, D Na+.
steps: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 has 18 electrons.
Cl has 17 electrons, so Cl- has 18.
Al3+ has 10, N3- has 10, Na+ has 10.

questions.question: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of magnesium? A Mg(g) -> Mg2+(g) + 2e-; B Mg+(g) -> Mg2+(g) + e-; C Mg(s) -> Mg2+(s) + 2e-; D Mg+(s) -> Mg2+(s) + e-.
steps: The second IE removes one electron from Mg+(g).
Ionisation energies refer to gaseous species.
Only option B fits.

questions.question: The numbers of subatomic particles in four species W, X, Y and Z are given in a table (not included in the extracted text). Which species are isotopic? Options A W and X, B W and Y, C X and Z, D Y and Z.
steps: Isotopes are atoms of the same element, so they have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
W (19 p, 20 n, 18 e) is K+ and X (19 p, 20 n, 19 e) is K, the same isotope with a different charge.
Y (20 p, 20 n, 18 e) is Ca2+ and Z (20 p, 22 n, 20 e) is Ca: same protons, different neutrons, so Y and Z are isotopic.

questions.question: The graph shows log(ionisation energy) against ionisation number for the successive ionisations of an element. How many quantum shells contain electrons, and how many electrons are in the outer shell? (The graph is not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: B: 3 quantum shells contain electrons and there are 5 electrons in the outer shell
steps: The graph has 15 points, so the atom has 15 electrons in all.
The first large jump comes between the 5th and 6th ionisations, so 5 electrons are in the outermost shell.
The second large jump comes between the 13th and 14th, so the next 8 electrons (6th to 13th) are in the second shell and the last 2 are in the first shell.
The structure is 2, 8, 5 (phosphorus): 3 shells with 5 outer electrons.

questions.question: Iodine has one isotope (mass number 127); chlorine has isotopes 35 and 37. How many molecular ion peaks are there in the mass spectrum of ICl3? Options A 2, B 3, C 4, D 5.
steps: Iodine gives one mass, so only chlorine isotopes change the molecular ion mass.
ICl3 can contain 0, 1, 2 or 3 atoms of 37Cl, each with 3 chlorine atoms.

questions.question: Which process occurs in region R of the mass spectrometer? Options A sample vaporised by heater, B electrons removed to form positive ions, C electrons added to form negative ions, D ions accelerated by an electric field. (The diagram is not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: B: electrons are removed from molecules or atoms and positive ions are formed
steps: Region R holds the heated filament (electron gun) and a positive plate, which is the ionisation region.
Fast electrons knock electrons off the sample, giving positive ions; the sample was already vaporised by the heater on the left.
Acceleration by an electric field takes place at the plates in region S, and T is the magnetic field.

questions.question: Which statement is correct for region T? A ions with a greater mass have a smaller deflection; B ions with a greater mass have a greater deflection; C ions with a greater charge have a smaller deflection; D ions are speeded up by a magnetic field.
steps: Region T is the magnetic field, which deflects the ion beam.
Radius of path r is proportional to mass x speed / (charge x field), so heavier ions have a larger radius (smaller deflection).
Greater charge gives greater deflection, and a magnetic field does not speed ions up, so A is correct.

questions.question: The Period 2 element with the highest melting temperature is: A aluminium, B boron, C carbon, D silicon.
steps: Aluminium, boron and silicon are not Period 2 elements except boron.
Carbon exists as a giant covalent lattice (diamond or graphite) with very strong covalent bonds.
Boron is also giant covalent but has a lower melting temperature (about 2350 C vs about 3550 C for carbon).

questions.topic: Relative Atomic Mass From Two Peaks
questions.question: The mass spectrum of a sample of an element has only two peaks. What is the approximate relative atomic mass? Options A 191.5, B 192.0, C 192.5, D 193.0. (The spectrum is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: The peaks are at m/z = 191 with abundance about 25 and m/z = 193 with abundance about 75.

questions.question: Which of these atoms has the most neutrons? (The options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number.
Tin-124 has the most neutrons (74).

questions.question: A stable ion M3+ contains 18 electrons. In which block of the Periodic Table is element M? Options A s, B p, C d, D f.
steps: M3+ has 18 electrons, so M has 21 electrons (atomic number 21).
Element 21 is scandium, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d1 4s2.
The last electron enters a 3d orbital, so M is in the d-block.

questions.question: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of chlorine? (The options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: The first IE gives Cl+(g), so the second removes one electron from Cl+(g).
The product is Cl2+(g) plus one electron.
Both species are gaseous, as ionisation energies are defined for gas-phase atoms and ions.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the electronic configuration of a sulfur atom in the ground state, including subshell labels.
questions.answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4 (3p has one pair and two singly occupied orbitals)
steps: Sulfur has 16 electrons.
Fill 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, leaving 4 electrons for 3p.
Hund's rule: 3p has three orbitals, so put one electron in each first (3 unpaired), then pair the fourth, giving 3p4 with one pair and two singles.

questions.question: Write an equation for the first ionisation energy of sulfur, including state symbols.
steps: The first ionisation energy removes one electron from one mole of gaseous atoms.
Reactant: S(g), product: S+(g) plus one electron e-.

questions.question: Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is less than those of both phosphorus and chlorine.
questions.answer: Sulfur's electron is removed from a 3p orbital that already contains a pair, so electron-electron repulsion makes it easier to remove. Phosphorus has a stable half-filled 3p3 and chlorine has higher nuclear charge.
steps: Compared with P (3p3, half-filled and stable), S removes an electron from a 3p orbital that already holds a pair.
Repulsion between the paired electrons makes that electron easier to remove, lowering the IE of S.
Compared with Cl, S has a lower nuclear charge (16 vs 17 protons) with the same shielding, so Cl is held more strongly.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term isotopes, in terms of subatomic particles.
questions.answer: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons (so different mass numbers).
steps: Isotopes are atoms of the same element, so they have the same number of protons.
They have different numbers of neutrons, which gives different mass numbers.
They have the same electron arrangement, so the same chemical properties.

questions.question: A sample of sulfur contains four isotopes (abundance data not included in the extracted text). Calculate the relative atomic mass to two decimal places.
steps: = 32.09 to two decimal places (32.0945).

questions.question: Calculate the number of sulfur atoms in the molecular ion shown in the mass spectrum of 32S (the spectrum is not included in the extracted text).
questions.answer: 8 sulfur atoms (the molecular ion is S8+ at m/z 256)
steps: The molecular ion is the peak with the largest m/z, which is at 256.
Each atom is 32S, so the number of atoms = 256 / 32 = 8.

questions.question: Suggest the formula of the most stable ion shown by the sulfur mass spectrum (the spectrum is not included in the extracted text).
steps: The most stable ion gives the largest (base) peak, which is the tallest peak at m/z = 64.
With 32S, 64 / 32 = 2 atoms, and the ion has a single positive charge, so the formula is S2+.

questions.question: In which series are the elements in order of increasing melting temperature? (The options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: B: Li (454 K) < Be (1560 K) < B (2349 K) < C (about 3800 K, giant covalent), so the melting temperatures increase through the series.
A decreases (I2 > Br2 > Cl2 > F2) because the London forces weaken with fewer electrons.
C decreases down Group 1 as metallic bonding weakens, and D (Si, P, S, Cl) falls after silicon.

questions.question: What is the total number of orbitals in a sulfur atom which contain at least one electron? Options A 3, B 5, C 8, D 9.
steps: Sulfur: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4.
Occupied orbitals: 1s (1), 2s (1), 2p (3), 3s (1), 3p (3, since 3p4 fills all three).

questions.question: Complete the electronic configurations of Cu and Cu2+ using [Ar].
steps: Cu is an exception: one 4s electron moves to 3d to give a full 3d10 subshell.
Cu: [Ar] 3d10 4s1.
Cu2+ loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d9.

questions.question: Complete the table of subatomic particles in the atoms of the copper isotopes 63Cu and 65Cu (table not included in the extracted text).
questions.answer: 63Cu: 29 protons, 34 neutrons, 29 electrons; 65Cu: 29 protons, 36 neutrons, 29 electrons
steps: Copper has atomic number 29, so both isotopes have 29 protons.
Neutrons = mass number - 29: 63 - 29 = 34 and 65 - 29 = 36.
Neutral atoms have electrons = protons = 29 for each isotope.

questions.question: Explain the term isotopes, using the information in the table for copper.
questions.answer: Isotopes of copper have the same number of protons (29) and electrons but different numbers of neutrons (34 and 36).
steps: Both isotopes of Cu have 29 protons, so they are the same element.
The 63Cu and 65Cu atoms have different numbers of neutrons (34 and 36).
Different mass numbers result from the different neutron numbers.

questions.question: State why the two copper isotopes have the same chemical reactions.
questions.answer: They have the same electronic configuration (same number of electrons), so the same outer electrons take part in bonding.
steps: Chemical reactions depend on the electrons, especially outer electrons.
Both isotopes have 29 electrons with the same configuration.
Neutrons do not affect chemical behaviour.

questions.question: The relative atomic mass of copper in a sample is 63.4. Calculate the percentage abundances of 63Cu and 65Cu, showing working.
steps: Let the abundance of 63Cu be x%, so 65Cu is (100 - x)%.
x = 80, so 63Cu is 80% and 65Cu is 20%.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction of solid copper(II) carbonate with dilute sulfuric acid. State symbols are not required.
steps: Carbonate plus acid gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Salt is copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4.
Balance: 1 Cu, 1 C, 1 S, 4 O and 2 H on each side.

questions.topic: Percentage Yield Of Hydrated Copper Sulfate
questions.question: 50.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid is reacted with copper(II) carbonate until no more reacts, giving 10.87 g of CuSO4.5H2O. Calculate the percentage yield to an appropriate number of significant figures. Mr CuSO4.5H2O = 249.6.
steps: Moles H2SO4 = 1.00 x 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol; acid is limiting since copper carbonate is used until no more reacts.
1 mol H2SO4 gives 1 mol CuSO4, which gives 1 mol CuSO4.5H2O, so theoretical moles = 0.0500 mol.
Theoretical mass = 0.0500 x 249.6 = 12.48 g.
Percentage yield = 10.87 / 12.48 x 100 = 87.1% (3 s.f., as 50.0 cm3 and 10.87 g have 3 s.f.).

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of a nitrogen atom? (Options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Nitrogen has 7 electrons (atomic number 7).
Fill 1s2 (2), 2s2 (4), then 2p3 (3 electrons, one in each 2p orbital).

questions.question: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of iodine? A I2(s) -> 2I+(g) + 2e-; B I2(g) -> 2I+(g) + 2e-; C 1/2 I2(s) -> I+(g) + e-; D I(g) -> I+(g) + e-.
steps: First IE is for one mole of gaseous atoms losing one electron.
Option D uses I(g) and I+(g) plus one electron.
A and B remove two electrons; C starts from solid iodine, which is not allowed.

questions.topic: Element With One Paired P Orbital
questions.question: Which element has only one p orbital containing a pair of electrons? Options A U, B V, C W, D X. (The graph of first ionisation energies is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: The pattern S < T < U > V < W < X, then a sharp fall to Y, shows X is neon (end of Period 2) and Y is sodium.
Working back: W = F, V = O, U = N, T = C, S = B, and the dip from U (N) to V (O) is the normal fall due to electron pairing.
Oxygen (2p4) has only one 2p orbital containing a pair; N has none, F has two and Ne has three. So the element is V.

questions.question: Which element is the least reactive? Options A S, B X, C Y, D Z. (The graph is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: X is the noble gas neon, at the peak of the graph.
It has a full outer shell and the highest first ionisation energy, so it is the least reactive.

questions.question: Which element has the greatest second ionisation energy? Options A S, B T, C X, D Y. (The graph is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Y is sodium, so Y+ has the stable noble-gas configuration 2s2 2p6.
Removing a second electron means removing one from a full inner shell, which is much closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so the energy is very large (about 4560 kJ mol^-1).
S (B), T (C) and X (Ne) have second ionisation energies of about 2430, 2350 and 3950 kJ mol^-1, all lower than that of Y.

questions.question: Give an equation that represents the first ionisation energy of lithium, including state symbols.
steps: First IE is for one mole of gaseous atoms losing one electron.
Lithium atom Li(g) forms Li+(g) plus one electron.

questions.question: Explain why there is a general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 2.
questions.answer: Nuclear charge increases across the period while shielding stays about the same (same shell), so the atomic radius decreases and the outer electrons are held more strongly.
steps: Across Period 2, protons are added to the same shell.
Shielding stays roughly the same because electrons are added to the same shell.
Greater effective nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer and more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove one.

questions.question: Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen.
questions.answer: Oxygen removes an electron from a 2p orbital that already contains a pair, so repulsion between paired electrons makes it easier to remove; nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p3.
steps: Nitrogen has 2p3 with one electron in each orbital, a stable half-filled arrangement.
Oxygen has 2p4, so one 2p orbital holds a pair of electrons.
Repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove, so O has a lower IE than N.

questions.question: All the successive ionisation energies of nitrogen are shown in a table (not included in the extracted text). Explain the trend in the successive ionisation energies of nitrogen.
questions.answer: Each successive IE is higher because electrons are removed from an increasingly positive ion, so the remaining electrons are held more strongly; there is a large jump when an electron is removed from a new, inner shell.
steps: Removing each electron leaves a more positive ion, so the nuclear attraction on the remaining electrons increases.
So each successive ionisation energy is larger than the one before.
A very large jump occurs after the 5 outer electrons are removed, because the next electron comes from the full inner 1s shell (nitrogen has 5 outer electrons).

questions.question: In which region of this mass spectrometer are the ions accelerated? Options A region P, B region Q, C region R, D region S. (The diagram is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: P is where the vaporised sample is ionised.
Q is the set of charged plates (grids) after the ioniser, where the positive ions are accelerated by an electric field.
R is the electromagnet that deflects the ions, and S is the detector.

questions.question: Four iron ions (54Fe+, 54Fe2+, 56Fe+, 56Fe2+) follow paths shown in a diagram. Which ion follows path 1? (The path diagram is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Deflection in a magnetic field is greatest for ions with the smallest mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).
Path 1 is the most deflected path, so it is taken by 54Fe2+ (the smallest m/z); path 4, the least deflected, is taken by 56Fe+.

questions.question: Naturally-occurring chlorine has isotopes 35Cl and 37Cl. How many peaks due to singly-charged molecular ions are seen in the mass spectrum of Cl2? Options A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
steps: Cl2 molecular ions can be 35Cl2 (m/z 70), 35Cl37Cl (m/z 72) and 37Cl2 (m/z 74).
Each is singly charged, so the m/z values are the masses.
Three distinct peaks.

questions.question: The element manganese has atomic number Z = 25. What are the numbers of s, p and d electrons in an atom of manganese? (Options are not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: 8 s electrons, 12 p electrons, 5 d electrons
steps: Mn configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s2.
s electrons: 1s2 + 2s2 + 3s2 + 4s2 = 8.
p electrons: 2p6 + 3p6 = 12; d electrons: 3d5 = 5.

questions.question: The atomic number of scandium is 21. What is the number of electrons in a scandium ion, Sc+? Options A 20, B 21, C 22, D 23.
steps: Sc has 21 electrons.
Sc+ has lost one electron.
21 - 1 = 20 electrons.

questions.question: Scandium (mass number 45) forms Sc+ and Sc2+ ions in a mass spectrometer. What is the m/z value of the peak due to Sc2+? Options A 22.5, B 33.0, C 45.0, D 90.0.
steps: Sc2+ has mass 45 and charge 2+.

questions.question: An atom of (symbol missing from the extracted text) forms a nitride ion, N3-. What are the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion?
steps: 15N has atomic number 7 (7 protons) and mass number 15, so 15 - 7 = 8 neutrons.
The neutral atom has 7 electrons; N3- has gained 3 electrons, giving 10 electrons.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of an oxygen atom in its ground state? (Options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Oxygen has 8 electrons (atomic number 8).
Fill 1s2 (2), 2s2 (4), then 2p4 (remaining 4 electrons: one pair and two singles).

questions.question: Which is the electronic configuration of chromium? (Options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Chromium has 24 electrons, so [Ar] (18) leaves 6 more.
Chromium is an exception: one 4s electron moves to 3d to give a half-filled 3d5.
Configuration: [Ar] 3d5 4s1.

questions.question: Which is a reason why fluorine has a higher first ionisation energy than oxygen? A fewer unpaired electrons; B fewer shells of electrons; C more electrons; D more protons.
questions.answer: D (more protons, so greater nuclear charge)
steps: F and O are both in Period 2, so they have the same number of shells.
F has one more proton, so greater nuclear charge in the same shell with similar shielding.
This holds the outer electrons more strongly, so the IE is higher.

questions.question: Which is the equation for the second ionisation of element J? A J(g) -> J2+(g) + 2e-; B J+(g) -> J2+(g) + e-; C J+(g) -> J3+(g) + 2e-; D J2+(g) -> J3+(g) + e-.
steps: The second IE removes one electron from the 1+ ion.
The reactant is J+(g) and the product is J2+(g) plus one electron.
Only B matches.

questions.question: How many neutrons and electrons are there in the ion shown? (The symbol and options are missing from the extracted text.)
steps: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 190 - 79 = 111.
The neutral atom has 79 electrons; Au2+ has lost 2, so 77 electrons.

questions.question: The first seven ionisation energies (kJ mol-1) of an element are 1010, 1900, 2910, 4960, 6270, 21 300 and 25 400. In which group is this element? Options A Group 3, B Group 4, C Group 5, D Group 6.
steps: The large jump is between the 5th (6270) and 6th (21 300) ionisation energies.
So there are 5 outer electrons, which means the element is in Group 5 (as labelled in the options).
After the 5th electron the next comes from a full inner shell, so the jump is large.

questions.question: The first ionisation energy of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus. Which is the best explanation? A atomic radius of S is greater than P; B electronegativity of S is greater than P; C repulsion between outer electrons of S is greater than P; D shielding by inner shell electrons of S is greater than P.
questions.answer: C (greater repulsion between outer electrons in S)
steps: S has 3p4, which has a pair of electrons in one 3p orbital; P has 3p3 with no pairs.
Repulsion between the paired electrons in S makes one easier to remove.
Atomic radius and electronegativity do not directly explain the lower IE, and shielding is similar.

questions.topic: Relative Formula Mass Of Basic Carbonate
questions.question: Calculate the relative formula mass of basic nickel(II) carbonate. (The formula is missing from the extracted text.)
steps: Formula: Ni3CO3(OH)4.4H2O.

questions.question: Calculate the atom economy by mass for the formation of basic nickel(II) carbonate by the reaction shown. (The equation is missing from the extracted text.)
steps: Mr of reactants: 3NiSO4 = 3 x 154.8 = 464.4; Na2CO3 = 106.0; 4NaOH = 160.0; 4H2O = 72.0; total = 802.4.
Desired product: Ni3CO3(OH)4.4H2O, Mr = 376.1 from part (i).

questions.question: Give the reason why the term 'relative molecular mass' is not appropriate for the compound in (a)(i).
questions.answer: Basic nickel(II) carbonate is an ionic compound with a giant lattice structure, not a molecule, so relative formula mass is used.
steps: Relative molecular mass applies only to simple molecular substances.
Basic nickel carbonate is ionic, with ions in a giant lattice rather than discrete molecules.
So the formula mass (relative formula mass) is the correct term.

questions.question: Give the electronic configuration of the nickel ion present in nickel(II) compounds.
steps: Ni has 28 electrons: [Ar] 3d8 4s2.
Ni2+ loses the two 4s electrons.
Ni2+ is [Ar] 3d8.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation for the formation of basic nickel(II) carbonate from nickel(II) sulfate. State symbols are not required. (The full equation is missing from the extracted text.)
steps: Remove the spectator ions Na+ and SO4 2- that appear unchanged on both sides.
The ions that react are 3Ni2+, CO3 2- and 4OH-, together with 4H2O, forming the solid product.
Charge check: left side 3 x (+2) + (-2) + 4 x (-1) = 0, matching the neutral solid.

questions.topic: Relative Formula Mass From Gas Volume
questions.question: 1.995 g of XSO4 reacts with excess Na2CO3 to form 150.0 cm3 of CO2 at r.t.p. (2XSO4 + 2Na2CO3 + H2O -> X2CO3(OH)2 + 2Na2SO4 + CO2). Calculate the relative formula mass of XSO4. Molar volume = 24.0 dm3 mol-1.
steps: From the equation, 2 mol XSO4 gives 1 mol CO2, so moles XSO4 = 2 x 0.00625 = 0.0125 mol.
This is the relative formula mass of XSO4.

questions.question: Deduce the identity of X, using your answer to (c)(i).
steps: The element with Ar 63.5 is copper, so X = Cu (CuSO4).

questions.question: An atom of (symbol and mass number missing from the extracted text) forms the ion Al3+. What are the numbers of protons, electrons and neutrons in this ion?
steps: 27Al has atomic number 13 (13 protons) and mass number 27, so 27 - 13 = 14 neutrons.
Al3+ has lost 3 electrons from the 13 in the atom, leaving 10 electrons.

questions.question: The mass spectrum of an element is shown. What is the relative atomic mass of this element? Options A 90.0, B 90.9, C 91.2, D 92.8. (The spectrum is not included in the extracted text.)
In which region of a mass spectrometer are particles ionised? Options A region P, B region Q, C region R, D region S. (The diagram is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: P is the inlet where the sample is vaporised and enters.
Q contains the electron gun (the filament coil), which bombards the vapour with high-energy electrons to form positive ions.
R is the acceleration region, followed by the magnetic field and the detector at S.

questions.question: A sample of chlorine, Cl2, is analysed in a mass spectrometer. Chlorine has two isotopes. What is the total number of peaks due to ions with a single positive charge? Options A two, B four, C five, D six.
steps: Molecular ions Cl2+: 35Cl2 (70), 35Cl37Cl (72), 37Cl2 (74), which gives 3 peaks.
Atomic ions Cl+ from fragmentation: 35Cl+ (35) and 37Cl+ (37), which gives 2 peaks.
Total = 3 + 2 = 5 peaks.

questions.topic: Shape And Capacity Of p Orbital
questions.question: What is the shape of a p orbital and the maximum number of electrons it can hold?
questions.answer: Dumbbell-shaped (two lobes); it holds a maximum of 2 electrons.
steps: A p orbital has two lobes on either side of the nucleus, a dumbbell shape.
Each orbital, whatever its type, holds at most 2 electrons with opposite spins.

questions.question: The electronic configurations of four elements are given. Which has the lowest first ionisation energy? A 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2; B 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1; C 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p2; D 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3.
steps: A (Mg, 3s2) has a full 3s subshell and a higher IE than Al.
B is Al, with one electron in 3p; this electron is in a higher-energy subshell further from the nucleus and is shielded, so its IE is lowest.
C (Si) and D (P) have higher nuclear charge and a more stable configuration, so higher IEs.

questions.question: Complete the electronic configuration for a bromine atom using s, p and d notation, starting from [Ar].
steps: Bromine has 35 electrons; argon has 18, leaving 17.
Fill 4s2 (2), 3d10 (10), 4p5 (5), totalling 17.
Configuration: [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p5.

questions.question: Complete the table of subatomic particles in a 79Br atom and an 81Br- ion.
questions.answer: 79Br: 35 protons, 44 neutrons, 35 electrons; 81Br-: 35 protons, 46 neutrons, 36 electrons
steps: Bromine has atomic number 35, so both have 35 protons.
79Br has 79 - 35 = 44 neutrons and 35 electrons (neutral).
81Br- has 81 - 35 = 46 neutrons and 35 + 1 = 36 electrons (1- ion).

questions.topic: Mass Spectrum Peaks Of Br2 Ions
questions.question: A sample of bromine has equal amounts of 79Br and 81Br. Complete the mass spectrum to show the peaks expected for Br2+ from this sample.
questions.answer: Three peaks at m/z 79, 80 and 81 in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 (from 79Br79Br, 79Br81Br and 81Br81Br, each 2+)
steps: Br2+ from 79Br2 has mass 158, so m/z = 158 / 2 = 79.
From 79Br81Br the mass is 160, so m/z = 80, and this is formed from both mixed pairs (twice as likely).
From 81Br2 the mass is 162, so m/z = 81.
Equal amounts of the two isotopes give peaks in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 at m/z 79, 80 and 81.

questions.question: Calculate the number of bromine molecules in 2.00 g of Br2. Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1. (Ar Br = 80.0.)

questions.topic: Moles Of Gas From Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: A sample of bromine gas occupies 200 cm3 at 77 C and 1.51 x 10^5 Pa. Using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K-1 mol-1, calculate the amount in moles of bromine molecules.
steps: Rearrange: n = pV / RT.

questions.question: Which is the electronic configuration of nitrogen? (Options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: Nitrogen has 7 electrons.
Fill 1s2 2s2, then 2p3 with one electron in each 2p orbital.

questions.topic: Maximum Electrons In Orbital And Shell
questions.question: What are the maximum numbers of electrons in a 2p orbital and in the third quantum shell?
questions.answer: 2 electrons in a 2p orbital; 18 electrons in the third shell
steps: A single orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons.
The third shell (n = 3) holds 2n2 = 18 electrons.

questions.question: Write the equation for the first ionisation energy of nitrogen, including state symbols.
steps: First IE: one mole of gaseous atoms loses one electron.
N(g) forms N+(g) and one electron.

questions.topic: First Ionisation Trends Atomic Numbers 3 To 10
questions.question: Explain the changes in first ionisation energy for the elements with atomic numbers 3 to 10. (The graph is not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: IE rises from Li to Be (nuclear charge increases in the same shell), falls at B (2p electron is higher in energy and more shielded than 2s), rises to N (increasing nuclear charge), falls at O (repulsion between paired 2p electrons), then rises to Ne.
steps: Li to Be: nuclear charge increases with the same shielding, so IE rises.
Be to B: the outer electron in B is a 2p electron, which is higher in energy and more shielded, so IE falls.
B to N: nuclear charge rises, so IE rises; N is more stable with a half-filled 2p3.
N to O: O's 2p electron is paired with another, causing repulsion, so IE falls; O to Ne then rises again with nuclear charge.

questions.question: Explain why the first ionisation energy of element 11 (sodium) is lower than that of element 3 (lithium).
questions.answer: The outer electron of sodium is in the 3rd shell, further from the nucleus and more shielded by two inner shells, whereas lithium's outer electron is in the 2nd shell with only 1s shielding.
steps: Na has its outer electron in the 3s subshell (n = 3); Li has its outer electron in 2s (n = 2).
Na has more inner shells (2 full shells), giving more shielding than Li (1 full shell).
The outer electron is further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted, so Na's IE is lower.

questions.question: Data from the mass spectrum of a sample of pure iron are given in a table. Which species is most likely to cause the peak at m/z = 28? Options A 28Fe+, B 56Fe2+, C 28Si+, D 84Sr3+.
steps: 28Fe+ cannot exist, since iron's isotopes have mass numbers 54 to 58.
Silicon (28Si+) would give m/z 28 but is not present, since the sample is pure iron.
56Fe2+ has m/z = 56 / 2 = 28 and is an iron species present in the sample, so it is the most likely cause.

questions.question: Which species contains 15 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons? A P3-, B P3+, C S2-, D S2+.
steps: 15 protons means phosphorus; mass number = 15 + 16 = 31.
18 electrons with 15 protons gives charge 15 - 18 = 3-, so P3-.
Sulfur has 16 protons, so C and D are not correct.

questions.question: A sample of neon contains the isotopes shown (not included in the extracted text). What is the relative atomic mass of neon to two decimal places? Options A 20.00, B 20.09, C 20.18, D 21.00.
steps: Relative atomic mass = (20 x 90.92 + 21 x 0.26 + 22 x 8.82) / 100.
= 20.18 to two decimal places (20.179).

questions.question: An atom of hydrogen is 1H. What is its mass in grams? Options A 1.6725 x 10^-24, B 1.6734 x 10^-24, C 3.3473 x 10^-24, D 3.3482 x 10^-24. (The table of particle masses is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: An atom of 1H has one proton and one electron and no neutron.
A omits the electron, C and D include a neutron that 1H does not have.

questions.question: Which of the particles would be deflected by an electric field? A electrons only; B electrons and protons only; C neutrons and protons only; D electrons, neutrons and protons.
steps: Electric fields deflect charged particles.
Electrons are negative and protons are positive, so both are deflected.
Neutrons have no charge and are not deflected.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of an atom of calcium? Options A [Ne] 3s1, B [Ar] 4s1, C [Ne] 3s2, D [Ar] 4s2.
steps: Calcium has 20 electrons; [Ar] accounts for 18.
The remaining 2 electrons go into 4s2.
Calcium is [Ar] 4s2.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of a Cr3+ ion? Options A [Ar] 3d2 4s1, B [Ar] 3d3, C [Ar] 3d4, D [Ar] 3d5.
steps: Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 (24 electrons).
Cr3+ loses 3 electrons: the 4s1 first, then 2 from 3d.

questions.question: Which pair of atomic numbers are those of elements in different blocks of the Periodic Table? A 5, 9; B 10, 16; C 13, 18; D 16, 20.
steps: Atomic number 5 (B) and 9 (F) are both p-block.
10 (Ne) and 16 (S) are both p-block; 13 (Al) and 18 (Ar) are both p-block.
16 (S) is p-block, while 20 (Ca) is s-block, so D is the pair in different blocks.

questions.question: Which species does not contain a total of 16 neutrons? A molecule of ethene, 12C2 1H4; B molecule of oxygen, 16O2; C atom of silicon, 30Si; D ion of sulfur, 32S2-.
steps: Neutrons = mass number - protons for each atom.
A: two 12C atoms have 6 neutrons each (12 total); 1H has none; total 12, not 16.
B: 2 x (16 - 8) = 16; C: 30 - 14 = 16; D: 32 - 16 = 16 (the 2- charge does not change neutrons).

questions.question: Define relative atomic mass.
questions.answer: The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element, compared to one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
steps: Relative atomic mass is a ratio, so it has no units.
It is the weighted mean of the masses of the naturally occurring isotopes.
It is compared to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.question: Calculate the relative atomic mass of a sample of silicon using the isotopic abundance data (the data are not included in the extracted text), to 3 significant figures.
In the mass spectrum of silicon there is also a small peak at m/z = 14. Deduce the formula of this particle.
steps: m/z = 14 with a 2+ charge gives a mass of 28.
28Si is the most abundant silicon isotope, so the particle is 28Si2+.
Formula: Si2+.

questions.topic: First Ionisation Trend Al Si P
questions.question: Explain the trend in the first ionisation energies of Al, Si and P.
questions.answer: IE increases from Al to Si to P because nuclear charge increases across Period 3 while shielding stays the same (same shell), so the outer electrons are held more strongly.
steps: Al, Si and P are in Period 3, with the outer electrons in the same shell.
Nuclear charge increases from Al (13) to Si (14) to P (15), with shielding about the same.
The effective nuclear attraction on the outer electrons increases, so more energy is needed to remove one.
Al is an exception to a strict rise: its outer electron is a 3p electron, higher in energy than 3s, so its IE is slightly lower than Mg, but Al to Si to P still rises.

questions.question: Explain why sulfur does not follow this trend in first ionisation energy.
questions.answer: Sulfur's outer electron is removed from a 3p orbital that already contains a pair, so repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove, lowering its IE.
steps: Sulfur has 3p4: one 3p orbital holds a pair of electrons.
Repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove.
This lowers S's first ionisation energy below that of P (3p3, no pairs).

questions.question: Which diagram represents the electronic structure of a nitrogen atom? (The diagram options are not included in the extracted text.)
questions.answer: C: 1s2 2s2 2p3 with one electron in each 2p orbital
steps: Nitrogen has 7 electrons: 1s2 2s2 2p3.
1s and 2s each hold a pair of opposite spins, and the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule).
A and B have only one electron in the 2s orbital; D puts a pair in one 2p orbital while another 2p is empty.

questions.question: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of magnesium? A Mg(g) -> Mg2+(g) + 2e-; B Mg+(g) -> Mg2+(g) + e-; C Mg+(s) -> Mg2+(s) + e-; D Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e-.
steps: The second IE removes an electron from Mg+(g), giving Mg2+(g).
Ionisation energies use gaseous species, which rules out C.
D is the first IE, and A removes two electrons together.

questions.question: Which values are the first four ionisation energies, in kJ mol-1, of gallium (Ga)? (Indium, germanium and tin are the other elements whose values appear among the options.) Options A 557 1821 2705 5200; B 579 1979 2963 6200; C 709 1412 2943 3930; D 762 1537 3302 4411.
steps: Gallium is in Group 13 with 3 outer electrons, so there should be a large jump after the 3rd IE.
Gallium's first IE is about 579 kJ mol-1 (standard data, as the table is not in the extracted text).
Option B has values rising steadily with a jump after the 3rd (2963 to 6200), matching Group 13.

questions.topic: Mass Number Of Fifth Germanium Isotope
questions.question: Germanium has five isotopes; the fifth is germanium-76 (radioactive). Calculate the mass number of the fifth isotope, given Ar = 72.6 and the data for the other four (table not included in the extracted text).
questions.answer: 72 (71.6 before rounding), so the fifth isotope is 72Ge
steps: The four isotopes in the table add up to 20.5 + 7.8 + 36.5 + 7.8 = 72.6%, so the fifth isotope has abundance 100 - 72.6 = 27.4%.
Sum for the four known isotopes: 70 x 20.5 + 73 x 7.8 + 74 x 36.5 + 76 x 7.8 = 5298.2.
Using Ar = 72.6: 72.6 x 100 = 7260, so the fifth isotope contributes 7260 - 5298.2 = 1961.8.
Mass number = 1961.8 / 27.4 = 71.6, which is 72.

questions.question: Give the main reason why the answer in (a)(i) should not be quoted to more than 2 significant figures.
questions.answer: The isotopic composition is only almost constant, and the relative atomic mass (72.6) is given to only one decimal place, so the calculated mass number is only approximate.
steps: The isotopic composition is described as only almost constant.
The Ar of 72.6 is only known to one decimal place, so the calculated value is limited in precision.
So the mass number cannot be quoted more precisely than about 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the atomic structure of germanium-76 with selenium-76, formed by radioactive decay of Ge-76.
questions.answer: Both have mass number 76 (same nucleons) and so the same total number of nucleons; Ge-76 has 32 protons and 44 neutrons, Se-76 has 34 protons and 42 neutrons; both have electrons equal to protons (32 and 34).
steps: Both have mass number 76, so the same total number of protons plus neutrons.
Ge has atomic number 32: 32 protons, 44 neutrons, 32 electrons.
Se has atomic number 34: 34 protons, 42 neutrons, 34 electrons.
Contrast: Se has 2 more protons and 2 fewer neutrons (and 2 more electrons) than Ge.

questions.question: Sulfur has a higher melting temperature than white phosphorus, P4. Which is a possible reason? A sulfur molecules have a greater permanent dipole than phosphorus molecules; B sulfur has stronger covalent bonds than phosphorus; C sulfur has a giant covalent structure and phosphorus has a simple molecular structure; D sulfur molecules have more electrons than phosphorus molecules.
questions.answer: D (sulfur molecules have more electrons, so stronger London forces)
steps: Both are non-polar simple molecular substances, so the forces are London (instantaneous dipole) forces.
S8 molecules have more electrons than P4, so stronger London forces between them.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the melting temperature is higher.

questions.question: Give the reason why the two electrons in the n = 1 energy level are represented by arrows pointing in opposite directions.
questions.answer: The two electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle).
steps: Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spin.
Opposite spins are shown by arrows in opposite directions.
This is the Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.

questions.topic: Energy Of Electrons In Second Shell
questions.question: Explain whether or not all of the electrons in the n = 2 energy level have the same energy.
questions.answer: No. The 2s and 2p electrons are in different subshells, and 2p electrons have a higher energy than 2s electrons.
steps: The n = 2 shell contains two subshells, 2s and 2p.
Electrons in the 2p subshell have higher energy than those in 2s.
So the electrons in n = 2 do not all have the same energy.

questions.question: Name the shape of the orbital occupied by the electron in the n = 3 energy level of sodium.
steps: Sodium is 2,8,1, so its single outer electron is in 3s.
An s orbital is spherical.

questions.question: Write the equation for the third ionisation energy of calcium, including state symbols.
steps: Calcium first forms Ca+ then Ca2+ on the first two ionisations.
The third IE removes one electron from Ca2+(g) to form Ca3+(g).
Gas-phase species, with one electron on the product side.

questions.question: The first seven ionisation energies for an element in Period 3 are shown (data not included in the extracted text). Deduce the identity of the element, with a reason.
questions.answer: Sulfur: there is a large jump between the 6th and 7th ionisation energies, so six outer electrons, giving Group 6 in Period 3
steps: The energies rise gradually from 1000 to 8496 kJ mol^-1 for the first six electrons.
There is a very large jump from the 6th (8496) to the 7th (27 107), so the 7th electron comes from an inner shell: the atom has 6 electrons in its outer shell.
An element in Period 3 with 6 outer electrons is in Group 6, sulfur (first ionisation energy about 1000 kJ mol^-1).

questions.question: State the general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3.
questions.answer: First ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3 (with small dips at Al and S).
steps: Nuclear charge increases across the period, with shielding about the same.
Outer electrons are held more strongly, so IE generally rises.
Small dips occur at Al (3p1) and S (paired 3p electrons).

questions.question: Explain the difference in first ionisation energies between beryllium and boron.
questions.answer: Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and more shielded than the 2s electrons of beryllium, so B has a lower first ionisation energy.
steps: Be has its outer electrons as a 2s2 pair; B's outer electron is in a 2p orbital.
The 2p subshell is higher in energy than 2s and is slightly further from the nucleus (more shielded).
So less energy is needed to remove B's 2p electron than a 2s electron from Be.

questions.question: Explain the difference in first ionisation energies between carbon and nitrogen.
questions.answer: Nitrogen has a higher IE because it has a stable, half-filled 2p3 subshell and higher nuclear charge; carbon's 2p2 has less stability and its outer electron is removed more easily.
steps: N has 7 protons and C has 6, so N has greater nuclear charge.
N has 2p3 (one electron per orbital), which is a stable half-filled subshell.
C has 2p2 with no half-filled stability, so its outer electron is easier to remove and C's IE is lower.

questions.topic: Neutrons And Electrons In Bromide Ion
questions.question: Which row shows the numbers of neutrons and electrons in a bromide ion, 79Br-? (The table of rows is not included in the extracted text.)
steps: 79Br has atomic number 35, so neutrons = 79 - 35 = 44.
The bromide ion Br- has gained 1 electron, so 35 + 1 = 36 electrons.

questions.question: Which is the correct order for the processes in a mass spectrometer? (The options are not included in the extracted text.)
steps: The sample must first be vaporised (turned into a gas).
It is then ionised (electron bombardment forms positive ions).
The ions are deflected by the magnetic field and finally detected.
